definitions.definition: Something that stays the same even when other things change.
definitions.example: The number of apples stays the same whether you arrange them in a circle or a line.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning the divine reason or order that makes the universe make sense.
definitions.example: Like the ultimate rulebook that everything in the universe follows.

definitions.definition: Different ways of showing the same thing from different angles.
definitions.example: A 3D object's shadow on a wall is a projection of it.

definitions.definition: A system for sorting things into groups based on their structure.
definitions.example: Like how scientists sort animals into mammals, birds, reptiles, etc.

definitions.definition: Something that must be true and cannot be false.
definitions.example: 2+2=4 is necessary; it couldn't be any other way.

definitions.definition: Not depending on anything else to be true.
definitions.example: The fact that a triangle has three sides doesn't depend on where you draw it.

definitions.definition: True no matter how you look at it or from where.
definitions.example: The speed of light is the same whether you're standing still or running.

definitions.definition: True no matter who is watching or measuring.
definitions.example: The mass of a rock doesn't change if you or I weigh it.

definitions.definition: True at all times, past, present, and future.
definitions.example: The law of gravity was true before humans existed and will be true after.

definitions.definition: True everywhere and for everyone without exception.
definitions.example: The rule that you can't divide by zero applies to all math, everywhere.

definitions.definition: Doesn't need to talk about itself to prove itself true.
definitions.example: A dictionary definition that doesn't use the word it's defining.

definitions.definition: Not having contradictions; all parts agree with each other.
definitions.example: A story where the character doesn't both win and lose the same race.

definitions.definition: Every statement in that area is either true or false, no in-between.
definitions.example: In arithmetic, every equation is either correct or incorrect.

definitions.definition: Can be found by anyone who honestly looks for it.
definitions.example: The answer to a math problem can be found by anyone who works it out.

definitions.definition: Learning one truth helps you learn more truths.
definitions.example: Once you know addition, it's easier to learn multiplication.

definitions.definition: Different paths lead to the same answer.
definitions.example: Adding 2+2 and multiplying 2x2 both give 4.

definitions.definition: When you find truth, it feels like remembering something you already knew.
definitions.example: When you finally understand a concept, it clicks like it was obvious all along.

definitions.definition: Cannot be destroyed or worn out.
definitions.example: A mathematical truth like 1+1=2 will never stop being true.

definitions.definition: Cannot be given to someone by making them accept it.
definitions.example: You can't force someone to understand a joke; they have to get it themselves.

definitions.definition: Has a natural hierarchy where some things depend on others.
definitions.example: You need to learn to add before you can learn algebra.

definitions.definition: Makes things fit together in a sensible way.
definitions.example: Putting puzzle pieces together so the picture makes sense.

definitions.definition: Not made true just because everyone agrees.
definitions.example: Even if everyone believed the Earth was flat, it would still be round.

definitions.definition: Not made true just because an expert says so.
definitions.example: A math problem is correct because of the numbers, not because the teacher says so.

definitions.definition: Open to being tested and possibly proven wrong.
definitions.example: A good scientist says 'Here's how you could prove my idea is wrong.'

definitions.definition: My having it doesn't take away from your having it.
definitions.example: If I know a song, you can still learn it too; the song isn't used up.

definitions.definition: Creates order instead of disorder.
definitions.example: Organizing a messy desk creates order, which is the opposite of entropy.

definitions.definition: Based on an ultimate source of order and truth outside itself.
definitions.example: Like a building that rests on solid bedrock, not on sand.

definitions.definition: Known only by accepting it as a gift, not by earning or making it.
definitions.example: You can't force yourself to feel loved; you have to receive love from someone else.

definitions.definition: Depends on something else to be true; could be false if conditions change.
definitions.example: Whether it's raining depends on the weather; it's not always true.

definitions.definition: Changes depending on how you look at it or from where.
definitions.example: Whether a ball is moving depends on whether you're standing still or running.

definitions.definition: Refers to itself to prove itself, which can cause problems.
definitions.example: This sentence is false' is self-referential and creates a paradox.

definitions.definition: A famous proof that any system strong enough to do arithmetic has truths it can't prove and might be inconsistent.
definitions.example: It shows that no single set of rules can explain everything in math.

definitions.definition: Says two things that cannot both be true at the same time.
definitions.example: Saying 'I am lying' is self-contradictory if you're telling the truth.

definitions.definition: Can be understood in more than one way; not clear.
definitions.example: The sentence 'I saw her duck' is ambiguous: did she lower her head or own a bird?

definitions.definition: Gets worse or less clear the more you look into it.
definitions.example: A mystery that gets more confusing the more clues you find.

definitions.definition: Different paths lead to different answers, and they don't come together.
definitions.example: If two people start at the same point and walk away in different directions, they get farther apart.

definitions.definition: Feels true because it's new and exciting, not because it's recognized as already true.
definitions.example: A new gadget feels amazing at first, but the feeling fades quickly.

definitions.definition: Can be destroyed or wears out over time.
definitions.example: Fruit left out will rot; it doesn't last forever.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get messier over time.
definitions.example: Your room gets messy on its own; cleaning it takes work.

definitions.definition: Can only be given to someone by making them accept it, not by them freely receiving it.
definitions.example: You can force someone to repeat a rule, but you can't force them to believe it.

definitions.definition: All things treated as equal in importance, with no hierarchy.
definitions.example: Saying that a child's opinion on rocket science is as valid as an engineer's.

definitions.definition: Makes things fall apart or not fit together.
definitions.example: Adding random parts to a machine that don't connect makes it break down.

definitions.definition: Only true as long as everyone agrees it is.
definitions.example: A game's rules are true only if players agree to follow them.

definitions.definition: Only true because someone in power says it is.
definitions.example: A law is true only because the government says it is; it can change.

definitions.definition: Avoids being tested or proven wrong.
definitions.example: A psychic who says 'my prediction failed because you doubted' is avoiding falsification.

definitions.definition: My having it means you can't have it; it's a limited resource.
definitions.example: If I eat the last cookie, you can't have it.

definitions.definition: Creates disorder or mess.
definitions.example: Dropping a box of Legos creates a mess; it doesn't organize itself.

definitions.definition: Claims to be its own source and authority, not relying on anything outside.
definitions.example: A person who says 'I am the only rule I need' is self-grounded.

definitions.definition: Refuses to accept truth as a gift; insists on earning or making it.
definitions.example: Someone who won't accept help because they want to do it all themselves.

definitions.definition: Tends to break down or fall apart over time because it's not orderly.
definitions.example: A sandcastle is thermodynamically unstable; waves will wash it away.

definitions.definition: Nine good qualities that come from being connected to God, listed in the Bible.
definitions.example: Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

definitions.definition: The specific pattern or sign that shows something is working a certain way.
definitions.example: A car's engine noise is the operational signature of how it's running.

definitions.definition: Signs or clues that help identify what something is.
definitions.example: A fever is a diagnostic marker of an infection.

definitions.definition: The idea that the nine Fruits of the Spirit always appear together or disappear together because they come from the same source.
definitions.example: If you have true love, you'll also have joy and peace; they come as a package.

definitions.definition: Appear together and disappear together.
definitions.example: Symptoms of a cold come and go as a group, not one at a time.

definitions.definition: The parts of a system that can be targeted or harmed.
definitions.example: A castle's gates are its attack surface; the walls are not.
